dedupe_keys.name: floods and hospitalisation risk in 747 communities of eight countries 2000 to 2019

description: This case study measures how floods change the risk of being admitted to hospital in the months after exposure. The authors, led by Monash University, published it as an open-access journal article. They collected daily hospitalisation counts from 2000 to 2019 in 747 communities in Australia, Brazil, Canada, Chile, New Zealand, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam, defined flooded days from the start and end dates of flood events, estimated lag-response associations with quasi-Poisson regression and distributed lag non-linear functions for each community, and pooled them with random-effects meta-analysis to compute attributable fractions. The article is free under a Creative Commons Attribution licence. Caveats: flood exposure is defined at community level from event records, hospitalisation data are not released with the article, and effects vary by climate and socio-economic context. Hospitalisation risks rose and persisted for up to 210 days after exposure, with relative risks of 1.26 for all causes, 1.35 for cardiovascular disease, 1.61 for diabetes and 1.40 for renal disease, and floods contributed up to 0.27 percent of all-cause hospitalisations. Simulation uses: estimating the lasting surge in hospital demand after floods for capacity planning and climate adaptation. Related records: the Kenya 2024 floods access study (case_study-kenya-2024-floods-healthcare-accessibility) covers loss of access, and the England heat admissions study (case_study-england-extreme-heat-hospital-admissions) covers heat.
